title: Missing Andy Kirk's Decca recording of Until the Real Thing Comes Along
summary: Tate declines Kirk's telegrams to record, and the song became a hit.

bands.name: Andy Kirk and His Clouds of Joy

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: So I -- oh, I'm a little ahead of my story. While I'm in Wylie, Andy Kirk's band, they hoboed back to Kansas City and Dick Wilson, who was a fine tenor saxaphone player, he's a stylist, actually, and he was with Zack White. But Andy called me, he sent three telegrams and says, "Look, we're going to record. The band's back together and I think we're going to make it." He says, "A guy coming down from Decca is going to record us and I want you to be on it."

So by this time, Gary, I didn't want to go through no more hard times. I was having a nice time there, you know. I just didn't go and I didn't regret it because later, I ended up with Basie, you know. But sure enough, they recorded "Until the Real Thing Comes Along." That was their big song, you know, with --

That was their first record. That was the one that -- no, they had made a record before then, but actually, it didn't make any noise, you know. They made a record in -- record date in the band like maybe two years before. But "Real Thing Came Along," -- we didn't call it that. We called it "The Slave Song." But you couldn't -- the fella said, "No, I can't put this on a record." You know how they were then about titles and lyrics and things. So he says, "No, I actually can't put this on a record." So sure enough, it wasn't no time before they sold a million. And I said to
myself, I says, "Buddy Tate, you're always at the wrong place."
